chunks: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man who is a narrator/transmitter of your hadiths, disseminating them among the people and fastening them into their hearts and the hearts of your Shia — and there is perhaps a worshipper from your Shia who does not have this narration — which of the two is superior?
He said: The narrator of our hadiths who fastens the hearts of our Shia with it is superior to a thousand worshippers.

key_terms.رَاوِيَة: A prolific narrator or transmitter of hadith; someone whose primary role is preserving and spreading the Imam's teachings
key_terms.عَابِد: A worshipper devoted to personal ritual devotion (prayer, fasting, etc.) without necessarily engaging in communal knowledge transmission
key_terms.يَبُثُّ: To disseminate, scatter, or spread widely — connoting active and broad transmission
key_terms.يُشَدِّدُ: To fasten firmly, strengthen, consolidate — the image of embedding belief deeply in the heart

ai.seo_question: Is transmitting hadith better than worship in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar poses a question to Imam al-Sadiq (AS) comparing two types of Shia: one who actively transmits and teaches the Imam's hadiths to strengthen the community's faith, and another who is devoted to personal worship but does not transmit knowledge. The Imam's answer elevates the transmitter of knowledge far above even a thousand worshippers, underscoring that disseminating the Imams' teachings is a communal obligation that multiplies spiritual merit immensely. This teaching addressed early Shia communities in Kufa and Medina, where preserving and transmitting the Imams' knowledge was critical for the community's religious survival under Abbasid suppression.
